{
  "command": "cd /Users/sumeet/matrix/elijah/.claude/worktrees/227 && gh pr create --base dev --head sumeet/run-cap-count-partial --draft --title \"Cross-FS: Count partial-state jobs against the run cap\" --body \"$(cat <<'EOF'\n## What this is\n\n`partial` job state was excluded from the run-cap count on the rationale \"don't punish the user for pipeline-side problems.\" But a partial run did all the expensive work — PDF retrieval, LLM driver extraction, indicator extraction, etc. — and only differs from succeeded in that one or more stages flagged quality issues. The user consumed the full pipeline budget; they should pay for the run.\n\nUser-facing symptom on staging today: `sumeetsaini621` has cap=3, one partial run, and one in-flight run, but the GUI quota chip says **\"2 of 3 runs remaining\"** — only counting the in-flight one. From the user's perspective they ran two questions, so the chip should say \"1 of 3 remaining.\"\n\nThis PR adds `partial` to `RUN_CAP_COUNTED_STATES`, updates the constant's docstring to make the include/exclude reasoning explicit, and extends the run-cap tests to cover the new behaviour.\n\n## Technical detail\n\n### Summary\n\n- `packages/storage/job_queue.py` — adds `\"partial\"` to `RUN_CAP_COUNTED_STATES` and rewrites the doc-comment to spell out which states count and which don't, with reasons:\n\n  | State | Counted? | Reason |\n  |---|---|---|\n  | `queued` | ✓ | submitted, charge on submit |\n  | `running` | ✓ | actively consuming pipeline budget |\n  | `succeeded` | ✓ | completed, full forecast |\n  | `partial` | **✓ (NEW)** | completed, gaps about analytical completeness — but full resource cost |\n  | `failed` | ✗ | pipeline crash, infra problem, not user's fault |\n  | `cancelled` | ✗ | user aborted; avoid double-disincentivising cancellation |\n  | `skipped` | ✗ | pipeline never ran (dedup, idempotency) |\n\n- `tests/test_run_cap.py` — `TestRunCapCountedStates.test_counted_states_include_partial` replaces the old strict-equality assertion, and a new `test_failed_and_cancelled_are_excluded` asserts the negative half. New integration test `test_partial_jobs_count` confirms a partial-state job rejects a 4th submission with 429.\n\n### Tests\n\n- `uv run python -m pytest tests/test_run_cap.py tests/test_api_demo_sentinel.py tests/test_job_queue_artifacts.py -x -q` → 30 passed (was 29; +1 new)\n- Full pytest running in background; will mark when green\n\n### Verification\n\n- [x] `uv run ruff check .`\n- [x] `uv run ruff format --check .`\n- [x] Run-cap tests pass with the new state included\n- [ ] Full pytest suite — running\n\n### Risks\n\n- Low. One-line behaviour change. The complementary side — what counts as a \"partial completion\" — is unchanged: `complete_job` continues to map a job to `partial` state when some stages flag quality issues; this PR just changes whether that partial run is counted against the cap.\n- A user who had been close to their cap with partial runs not counted could suddenly find themselves at the cap after this lands. That's the correct behaviour; the prior accounting was lenient and inconsistent with the quota chip's intent.\n\n### Branch-merge\n\nStandalone. No dependency on other in-flight PRs.\n\n### Out of scope (deliberately)\n\n- The GUI quota chip's display: no frontend changes needed; the chip already reads `me.used` from `/api/users/me` which calls `count_counted_jobs` — and `count_counted_jobs` already filters by `RUN_CAP_COUNTED_STATES`. So the chip will automatically reflect the new count after this lands.\n- Any retrospective adjustment to existing partial jobs in production DBs — none needed; the next time the count is read, it'll include partial rows automatically.\n\n@kungfusaini\nEOF\n)\" 2>&1 | tail -3",

def _infer_question_source(*, question_id: object, url: object, metadata: dict[str, Any] | None) -> str:
    explicit = metadata_text(metadata or {}, "question_source", "", aliases=("question_source", "source_tag"))

        return explicit
    question_id_text = str(question_id or "").strip().lower()

    return "unknown"


def _normalize_loaded_edge_type(edge_type: object) -> str | None:

    UI/Workspaces: Stack disconnected info nodes in analyst graph (#326)
    
    ELK's layered algorithm ranks nodes by edge structure, so information
    nodes with no incoming or outgoing edges get packed as a disconnected
    grid block above the rest of the graph instead of sitting in the
    leftmost rank like the established layout.
    
    Add a post-layout pass in runLayout's layoutstop handler that always
    stacks visible information nodes in a single vertical column to the
    left of the other nodes, sorted by data.order then id. Row spacing and
    column offset reuse the existing layoutSpacing controls so the Spacing
    buttons still affect it. When the layout-grouping toggle aggregates
    info nodes into one bubble the pass is a no-op for the aggregate.

+      // Information nodes are the leftmost rank in the explorer's vocabulary,
+      // but the real backend doesn't always emit `information -> driver`
+      // reference edges. When those edges are missing ELK has no anchor for
+      // the info nodes and dumps them as a packed grid block above the rest
+      // of the graph. Force them into a single vertical column on the left
+      // so the layout stays consistent whether or not the reference edges

+        const infoNodes = cy.nodes('[type = "information"]')
+          .filter((node) => !node.hasClass("grouped-out"));

+        const otherNodes = cy.nodes()
+          .filter((node) => node.data("type") !== "information" && !node.hasClass("grouped-out"));

+          const ob = b.data("order");

+          const otherXs = otherNodes.map((node) => node.position("x"));
+          const otherYs = otherNodes.map((node) => node.position("y"));
+          x = Math.min(...otherXs) - columnGap;
+          centerY = (Math.min(...otherYs) + Math.max(...otherYs)) / 2;
+        } else {
+          x = 0;
+          centerY = 0;
+        }
+        const totalHeight = (sorted.length - 1) * rowSpacing;
+        const startY = centerY - totalHeight / 2;
+        sorted.forEach((node, index) => {
+          node.position({ x, y: startY + index * rowSpacing });
+        });
+      }

Force them into a single vertical column on the left\n      // so the layout stays consistent whether or not the reference edges\n      // were materialized.\n      function stackInformationNodes() {\n        const infoNodes = cy.nodes('[type = \"information\"]')\n          .filter((node) => !node.hasClass(\"grouped-out\"));\n        if (infoNodes.length === 0) return;\n        const otherNodes = cy.nodes()\n          .filter((node) => node.data(\"type\") !== \"information\" && !node.hasClass(\"grouped-out\"));\n        const sorted = infoNodes.sort((a, b) => {\n          const oa = a.data(\"order\");\n          const ob = b.data(\"order\");\n          if (Number.isFinite(oa) && Number.isFinite(ob) && oa !== ob) return oa - ob;\n          return String(a.id()).localeCompare(String(b.id()));\n        });\n        const rowSpacing = layoutSpacing.vertical;\n        const columnGap = layoutSpacing.horizontal;\n        let x;\n        let centerY;\n        if (otherNodes.length > 0) {\n          const otherXs = otherNodes.map((node) => node.position(\"x\"));\n          const otherYs = otherNodes.map((node) => node.position(\"y\"));\n          x = Math.min(...otherXs) - columnGap;\n          centerY = (Math.min(...otherYs) + Math.max(...otherYs)) / 2;\n        } else {\n          x = 0;\n          centerY = 0;\n        }\n        const totalHeight = (sorted.length - 1) * rowSpacing;\n        const startY = centerY - totalHeight / 2;\n        sorted.forEach((node, index) => {\n          node.position({ x, y: startY + index * rowSpacing });\n        });\n      }",
  "new_string": "      // Information nodes are the leftmost rank in the explorer's vocabulary,\n      // but the real backend doesn't always emit `information -> driver`\n      // reference edges. When those edges are missing ELK has no anchor for\n      // the info nodes and dumps them as a packed grid block above the rest\n      // of the graph. Force them into vertical columns on the left so the\n      // layout stays consistent whether or not the reference edges were\n      // materialized.\n      //\n      // Two columns, read left-to-right:\n      //   1. Orphan column — info nodes with NO edges. These are the bits of\n      //      retrieved evidence the pipeline couldn't link back into the\n      //      analytical graph; surfacing them first signals \"here's stuff we\n      //      pulled in but didn't wire up.\"\n      //   2. Connected column — info nodes that DO have at least one edge.\n      //      These attach to drivers/indicators in the main graph and sit\n      //      one columnGap to the right of the orphan column so the visual\n      //      flow is \"evidence we collected → evidence that's actually\n      //      supporting the analysis → analysis itself.\"\n      function stackInformationNodes() {\n        const infoNodes = cy.nodes('[type = \"information\"]')\n          .filter((node) => !node.hasClass(\"grouped-out\"));\n        if (infoNodes.length === 0) return;\n        const otherNodes = cy.nodes()\n          .filter((node) => node.data(\"type\") !== \"information\" && !node.hasClass(\"grouped-out\"));\n\n        // Partition into orphan (no incident edges) vs connected. Use Cytoscape's\n        // connectedEdges() so we count edges from BOTH sides — an info node only\n        // counts as connected if it has at least one neighbour beyond itself.\n        const orphanNodes = infoNodes.filter((node) => node.connectedEdges().length === 0);\n        const connectedNodes = infoNodes.filter((node) => node.connectedEdges().length > 0);\n\n        const sortStacked = (collection) =>\n          collection.sort((a, b) => {\n            const oa = a.data(\"order\");\n            const ob = b.data(\"order\");\n            if (Number.isFinite(oa) && Number.isFinite(ob) && oa !== ob) return oa - ob;\n            return String(a.id()).localeCompare(String(b.id()));\n          });\n\n        const rowSpacing = layoutSpacing.vertical;\n        const columnGap = layoutSpacing.horizontal;\n\n        // Anchor both columns relative to the main graph. Orphan column sits\n        // 2x columnGap left of the leftmost other-node; connected column sits\n        // 1x columnGap left (between orphans and the main graph).\n        let connectedX;\n        let orphanX;\n        let centerY;\n        if (otherNodes.length > 0) {\n          const otherXs = otherNodes.map((node) => node.position(\"x\"));\n          const otherYs = otherNodes.map((node) => node.position(\"y\"));\n          const leftmost = Math.min(...otherXs);\n          connectedX = leftmost - columnGap;\n          orphanX = leftmost - 2 * columnGap;\n          centerY = (Math.min(...otherYs) + Math.max(...otherYs)) / 2;\n        } else {\n          // No main graph yet (rare — only if every node is information AND\n          // every info node is orphaned). Use two arbitrary columns near 0.\n          connectedX = 0;\n          orphanX = -columnGap;\n          centerY = 0;\n        }\n\n        const stack = (collection, x) => {\n          if (collection.length === 0) return;\n          const sorted = sortStacked(collection);\n          const totalHeight = (sorted.length - 1) * rowSpacing;\n          const startY = centerY - totalHeight / 2;\n          sorted.forEach((node, index) => {\n            node.position({ x, y: startY + index * rowSpacing });\n          });\n        };\n\n        stack(orphanNodes, orphanX);\n        stack(connectedNodes, connectedX);\n      }"
}

Same function, slightly more arithmetic. The orphan vs connected partition uses Cytoscape's `connectedEdges()` which returns edges incident from either side — an info node only ends up in the connected column if it has at least one real neighbour in the rendered graph.\n\n### Branch-merge\n\nStandalone. Could come later if you want explicit labels rather than positional encoding.\n- Re-layout when an edge is added/removed manually. The pass only runs on `layoutstop`; toggling the layout-grouping picker or hitting a Spacing button retriggers it.   "new_string": "        // Pull the real graph for the active question and re-render the\n        // cytoscape canvas. /api/questions/{id}/graph returns\n        // {question, nodes, edges, summary} — `refreshGraphFromData`\n        // normalises the nodes/edges against the shim shape;\n        // `refreshPredictionHeroFromSummary` reads the QuestionSummaryRead\n        // (options + prior + posterior arrays) and updates the hero card.\n        //\n        // Optional `runId` scopes the fetched graph to a specific run via\n        // the API's `?run_id=` query param (see services/api/routes/graphs.py).\n        // Omitted on the initial load (which shows the latest/composite\n        // graph) and passed by the run-history change handler so picking a\n        // prior run actually re-renders that run's nodes/edges/summary.\n        async function refreshGraphForQuestion(questionId, runId = null) {\n          const base = `/api/questions/${encodeURIComponent(questionId)}/graph`;\n          const url = runId ? `${base}?run_id=${encodeURIComponent(runId)}` : base;\n          const graphPayload = await fetchJson(url);\n          if (!graphPayload) return;\n          refreshGraphFromData(graphPayload);\n          // Only populate the Prediction hero with the summary when the\n          // active question actually has a completed run; otherwise the\n          // hero is hidden and the empty-state card is showing, so\n          // writing into the hidden hero would just stash stale numbers.\n          if (graphPayload.summary && analystState.activeQuestionHasCompletedRun) {\n            refreshPredictionHeroFromSummary(graphPayload.summary);\n          }\n        }"

```json
{
  "command": "gh pr create --base dev --head sumeet/analyst-reload-graph-on-run-change --draft --title \"FS-Workspaces: Reload graph scoped to selected run on run-history change\" --body \"$(cat <<'EOF'\n## What this is\n\nPicking a prior run from the run-history dropdown moved the prediction-source line and the job-status stepper but didn't re-fetch the graph — so the cytoscape canvas kept showing whatever was last loaded. Switching runs visually looked like nothing happened.\n\nThe backend already supports per-run graph scoping (`GET /api/questions/{id}/graph?run_id=...`). This PR threads it through the GUI so picking a run actually re-renders that run's nodes/edges/summary.\n\n## Technical detail\n\n### Summary\n\nTwo changes in `frontend/analyst/index.html`:\n\n1. `refreshGraphForQuestion(questionId, runId = null)` builds the URL with `?run_id=...` when a run is supplied, omits it otherwise. Initial page load + question-switch keep calling without `runId` (composite/latest view), the run-history change handler calls with the selected run's id.\n2. New change handler on `runHistorySelect` reads the option's value (which already holds `run_id || job_id` from `refreshRunHistory`) and calls `refreshGraphForQuestion(questionId, runId)`. Skips the \"no runs yet\" placeholder option (empty value).\n\nThe existing wireframe change handler at line 3153 still updates the prediction-source line + job-status stepper from the option's dataset; this PR adds the data refresh alongside.\n\n### Tests\n\nExtends `test_analyst_workspace_ships_graph_refresh_wiring` to pin both halves:\n- The function signature `refreshGraphForQuestion(questionId, runId = null)` exists in the served HTML\n- The `?run_id=` URL construction exists in the served HTML\n\n### Verification\n\n- [x] `uv run ruff check .`\n- [x] `uv run ruff format --check .`\n- [x] `uv run python -m pytest tests/test_api_service.py -k \"workspace or analyst\" -x -q` → 6 passed\n- [x] Headless Playwright load of `/analyst/`: 0 page errors, all three cytoscape canvases paint\n\n### Risks\n\nLow. Frontend-only change. The API endpoint contract is unchanged (the `?run_id=` query param already existed). If a future caller passes a stale or invalid run_id, the API returns the same empty-graph response it would for any unknown id — the page handles that gracefully via the existing `if (!graphPayload) return` guard.\n\n### Branch-merge\n\nStandalone. No dependency on other in-flight PRs.\n\n### Out of scope (deliberately)\n\n- A visual treatment for \"the loaded graph is from a prior run, not the latest\" — currently the only signal is the run-history dropdown's own selection. Could add a banner like \"Viewing run from 2026-05-21 09:28\" if you want it explicit.\n- Re-scoping the prediction hero / Probability Forecast to the per-run summary. Today those still use the `summary` block from the same fetch, so they will update to the per-run summary automatically — but if a run-scoped summary isn't in the response (some older runs may not have one) the hero stays on whatever was previously rendered.\n\n@kungfusaini\nEOF\n)\" 2>&1 | tail -3",
  "description": "Open PR"
}

---

## Adding a new user to the demo

Two layers — Cloudflare Zero Trust (lets them reach the URL) and `api_users.toml` on Betty (sets their cap or admin status). The toml step is **optional** — anyone added to the CF policy gets the default cap automatically.

### 1. Cloudflare Zero Trust — required

This is what gates access to the staging URL at the edge. Without an email in the CF policy, the user gets the Cloudflare login wall and can't reach the app at all.

1. Open Cloudflare Zero Trust dashboard
2. Access → Applications → find the staging app
3. Open the **"Demo Users"** policy
4. Add the new user's email under the "Include" rule
5. Save

That's enough. The user can now log into the workspace and they'll be auto-provisioned as a **non-admin** with the default **10-run** lifetime cap.

### 2. `api_users.toml` on Betty — optional, only if non-default

If the default 10-run non-admin cap is fine, **stop here** — you don't need to touch the toml.

Touch the toml only if you want to:
- Give them **admin** (uncapped, sees everyone's jobs)
- Give them a **custom cap** different from the default 10

Edit `/home/elijah/staging/elijah-config/api_users.toml` on Betty. The file is bind-mounted into the API container, so it survives redeploys.

**To add an admin** (append to the Admins block):

```toml
[[users]]
user_id = "alice"
name    = "Alice"
email   = "alice@example.com"
admin   = true
```

**To add a custom-capped user** (append to the Capped demo users block):

```toml
[[users]]
user_id  = "bob_external"
name     = "Bob (External)"
email    = "bob@example.com"
max_runs = 25
```

Then reload the API so it re-reads the toml:

```bash
ssh elijah
docker cp /home/elijah/staging/elijah-config/api_users.toml elijah-staging-api-1:/app/config/api_users.toml
docker compose -f /home/elijah/staging/compose.staging.yml restart api
```

### Notes

- **`user_id`** is just a stable internal handle — it shows up in the GUI's "submitted by" column on jobs. Convention: lowercase, underscore-separated. Doesn't have to match anything.
- **`email`** must match exactly what Cloudflare passes in the `Cf-Access-Authenticated-User-Email` header. Case-insensitive on the loader side, but be consistent.
- **Admin users**: uncapped (no `max_runs` field), see every user's jobs in the workspace, can delete demo questions.
- **Non-admin users**: see only their own jobs (plus any tagged `submitted_by='demo'`). `max_runs` is a **lifetime** cap, not a per-day quota.
- **Removing access**: drop them from the CF policy. The toml entry is harmless if left — it only takes effect if they ever come through CF again.

### Quick verification

```bash
# As the user (replace with their email):
ssh elijah "docker exec elijah-staging-api-1 curl -s \
  -H 'X-API-Key: <STAGING_API_KEY>' \
  -H 'Cf-Access-Authenticated-User-Email: new.user@example.com' \
  http://localhost:8000/api/users/me"
```

Returns `{user_id, email, is_admin, max_runs, used}` — confirms what cap and admin status the user resolves to.

276	        def _serve_workspace_html(request: Request, file_path) -> HTMLResponse:
277	            """Serve a workspace HTML file with two server-known values
278	            injected as window globals:
279	
280	            * ``window.ELIJAH_USER_EMAIL`` — the signed-in user from
281	              the ``Cf-Access-Authenticated-User-Email`` request header
282	              (set by Cloudflare Zero Trust at the edge). Replaces the
283	              placeholder identity in the topbar / sidebar.
284	            * ``window.ELIJAH_API_KEY`` — the API key configured for
285	              this app instance, so the workspace's ``fetch`` calls
286	              can pass ``X-API-Key`` against the same origin. Mirrors
287	              the long-standing pattern in ``frontend_index`` for the
288	              legacy UI.
289	
290	            When a value isn't available (header absent, API auth
291	            disabled), the corresponding global is simply not set and
292	            the wireframe falls back to its static placeholder copy.
293	            """
294	            html = file_path.read_text()
295	            inserts = []
296	
297	            user_email = (request.headers.get("Cf-Access-Authenticated-User-Email") or "").strip()
298	            if user_email:
299	                # JSON-encode the email and additionally escape `</` so a
300	                # value containing `</script>` can't terminate the
301	                # surrounding script tag. CF Access only forwards verified
302	                # emails so this is defence in depth.
303	                safe_email = json.dumps(user_email).replace("</", "<\\/")
304	                inserts.append(f"window.ELIJAH_USER_EMAIL={safe_email};")
305	
306	            if resolved_config.api_key:
307	                safe_api_key = json.dumps(resolved_config.api_key).replace("</", "<\\/")
308	                inserts.append(f"window.ELIJAH_API_KEY={safe_api_key};")
309	
310	            if inserts:
311	                inject = f"<script>{''.join(inserts)}</script>"
312	                html = html.replace("</head>", f"{inject}</head>", 1)
313	            return HTMLResponse(content=html)

{

  "content": "# Adding a new user to the demo\n\nTwo layers — Cloudflare Zero Trust (lets them reach the URL) and\n`api_users.toml` on Betty (sets their cap or admin status). The toml step is\n**optional** — anyone added to the Cloudflare policy gets the default\nauto-provisioned cap automatically.\n\n## 1. Cloudflare Zero Trust — required\n\nGates access to the staging / prod URL at the edge. Without an email in the\nCloudflare policy, the user hits the Cloudflare login wall and can't reach\nthe app at all.\n\n1. Open the **Cloudflare Zero Trust** dashboard.\n2. **Access → Applications →** find the staging or prod app.\n3. Open the **\"Demo Users\"** policy.\n4. Add the new user's email under the \"Include\" rule.\n5. Save.\n\nThat's enough. The user can now sign in via Cloudflare. On first request\nthey're auto-provisioned as a **non-admin** with the default lifetime run\ncap (see `[defaults].max_runs` in the toml — currently `10`).\n\n## 2. `api_users.toml` — optional, only if non-default\n\nIf the default cap is fine, **stop here** — you don't need to touch the\ntoml.\n\nTouch the toml only if you want to:\n\n- Give the user **admin** (uncapped, sees every user's jobs in the GUI,\n  can delete demo questions).\n- Give them a **custom cap** different from `[defaults].max_runs`.\n\nThe toml lives at `/home/elijah/<env>/elijah-config/api_users.toml` on\nBetty, bind-mounted into the API container per `compose.<env>.yml`. Edits\nto the host file survive redeploys.\n\n### To add an admin\n\nAppend to the *Admins* block:\n\n```toml\n[[users]]\nuser_id = \"alice\"\nname    = \"Alice\"\nemail   = \"alice@example.com\"\nadmin   = true\n```\n\n### To add a custom-capped non-admin\n\nAppend to the *Capped demo users* block:\n\n```toml\n[[users]]\nuser_id  = \"bob_external\"\nname     = \"Bob (External)\"\nemail    = \"bob@example.com\"\nmax_runs = 25\n```\n\n### Reload after editing\n\nThe loader reads the toml once at startup, so restart the API service\nafter editing:\n\n```bash\nssh elijah\ndocker cp /home/elijah/staging/elijah-config/api_users.toml \\\n  elijah-staging-api-1:/app/config/api_users.toml\ndocker compose -f /home/elijah/staging/compose.staging.yml restart api\n```\n\n(Replace `staging` with `prod` for the prod environment.)\n\nThe `docker cp` step is needed because the loader inside the container\nreads from `/app/config/api_users.toml`, not from the bind-mount path\ndirectly — the bind mount provides persistence across deploys; the cp\ngets the file into the running container's view.\n\n## Field reference\n\n| Field | Required | Notes |\n|---|---|---|\n| `user_id` | yes | Stable internal handle. Shows up in the GUI's \"submitted by\" column on jobs. Convention: lowercase, underscore-separated. Doesn't have to match anything external. |\n| `email` | yes | Must match what Cloudflare passes in the `Cf-Access-Authenticated-User-Email` header. Case-insensitive on the loader side, but be consistent. |\n| `name` | no | Human-readable name. Falls back to `user_id` if omitted. |\n| `admin` | no (default `false`) | Admins are uncapped, see every user's jobs, and can delete demo questions. Don't set `max_runs` on admins — they ignore it. |\n| `max_runs` | no | Lifetime cap on counted job states (`queued` / `running` / `succeeded` / `partial`). Omit to make the user uncapped (typical for admins). |\n| `api_key` | no | Per-user API key for programmatic callers. Not used by the demo; the shared `ELIJAH_API_KEY` env var handles that case. |\n\n## Removing access\n\nDrop the user from the Cloudflare \"Demo Users\" policy. The toml entry is\nharmless if left behind — it only takes effect if they ever come through\nCloudflare again.\n\n## Verifying a new user resolves correctly\n\nFrom Betty, simulate the user's request and inspect the resolved identity:\n\n```bash\nssh elijah\ndocker exec elijah-staging-api-1 curl -s \\\n  -H 'X-API-Key: <STAGING_API_KEY>' \\\n  -H 'Cf-Access-Authenticated-User-Email: new.user@example.com' \\\n  http://localhost:8000/api/users/me\n```\n\nReturns `{user_id, email, is_admin, max_runs, used}`. Confirms:\n\n- The user was found in the registry (their explicit `user_id` and\n  `is_admin` show up) OR auto-provisioned (`user_id` matches the email).\n- The cap they actually see (`max_runs`).\n- Their current usage (`used`).\n\nIf you get back `max_runs: null` for someone you expected to be capped,\ncheck that their email in the toml matches the one Cloudflare passes\nexactly, and that the API service was restarted after the edit.\n"
}

> DEVELOPER

what happens if a user is not added tot he toml file but they have access in cloudflare. Do they still see their email on the top of the screen in the gui or what

> AGENT

Yes — they see their email in the nav, just like an explicit user. Here's the flow end to end:

1. **CF Access** authenticates them at the edge and forwards their email in the `Cf-Access-Authenticated-User-Email` header on every request.
2. **API server-side injection**: when serving `/analyst/`, the `_serve_workspace_html` helper reads that header and splices `window.ELIJAH_USER_EMAIL = "<email>"` into the HTML before `</head>`.
3. **Frontend** reads `window.ELIJAH_USER_EMAIL` and populates the `#brandIdentityEmail` element under the Elijah brand title.
4. **`/api/users/me`** doesn't find them in the registry → auto-provisions a synthetic `User` with `user_id = email`, `is_admin = false`, `max_runs = 10` (from `[defaults]`). The quota chip below the email reads from this and shows "X of 10 runs left".

So a CF-only user sees exactly the same chrome as someone explicitly listed in the toml — email + quota chip — they just get the default cap and non-admin scope by default. The only operational differences vs an explicit toml entry:

- `user_id` defaults to their full email (e.g. `newcomer@example.com`) instead of a friendly handle (e.g. `alice`)
- They're never admin (auto-provisioning hardcodes `is_admin = false`)
- They use `[defaults].max_runs` rather than a custom cap

Functionally identical from their POV; they wouldn't know they weren't explicitly listed.

> AGENT

The two sides diverged in opposite directions:

- **main** grew the seed to **3,567 lines** — added 20 GJOpen questions with graphs/nodes/edges
- **dev** shrank it to **621 lines** — clean "ported baseline" from SPI-237 PR1
- **merge-base** was 686 lines (so dev is roughly at the original, main expanded heavily)

**Why this happened:** main got direct commits (the GJOpen seed expansion) that never came back into dev. Standard workflow drift bug; nothing we can fix at merge time except pick a winner.

**Practical impact:** the seed file runs only on a *fresh* Postgres volume (it's mounted to `docker-entrypoint-initdb.d`). Prod's volume persists across deploys, so this PR's seed change won't actually do anything to prod's existing data. Same goes for staging. The seed only matters for brand-new dev envs and CI's docker tests.

**My recommendation: take dev's version.** Reasons:

1. Dev's smaller "ported baseline" has been running on staging for weeks
2. Dev is supposed to be the integration branch — those main-only commits should never have happened
3. The 20 GJOpen questions main added aren't on dev anywhere; we've been seeding test data via the UK CPI script instead
4. Smaller seed = faster fresh-DB bring-up

**Alternative if you want to keep the GJOpen 20:** I can resolve by taking dev's port AS WELL AS re-applying the GJOpen-20 inserts on top (more work, two-step resolution, but preserves that content for any future fresh-env spin-up).

Which? Take-dev (simple), or merge-both (preserve GJOpen seed)?

can you work me tthoughtwhat the differents are between squash, merge commits etc

> AGENT

Three options on most GitHub repos. They all end up "applying the PR to the base branch" but differ in what gets recorded.

## The setup

Imagine PR with 3 commits (A, B, C) going from `feature` into `main`. Before merging:

```
main:    M1 ──── M2
                  \
feature:           A ──── B ──── C
```

## 1. Squash and merge

GitHub takes all the diffs from A+B+C, collapses them into ONE new commit, and lands that on main.

```
main:    M1 ──── M2 ──── S    (S = single commit with squashed content)
```

- `S` has **one parent** (M2)
- A, B, C disappear from main's history
- Commit message defaults to PR title (you can override)

**Pros:** clean main history — one commit per PR, easy to scan, easy to revert ("git revert S" undoes the whole PR).
**Cons:** loses fine-grained history. A, B, C still exist on the `feature` branch but are "orphaned" from main's perspective.

**This is the GitHub default for most repos. It's what bit us on #334.**

## 2. Create a merge commit

GitHub preserves A, B, C as-is and adds a **merge commit** that has TWO parents — main's previous tip AND the feature branch's tip.

```
main:    M1 ──── M2 ──────────────── M3
                  \                  /
feature:           A ──── B ──── C ─
```

- `M3` has **two parents** (M2 and C)
- A, B, C are now in main's history
- The merge commit's existence tells git "everything reachable from C is now part of main"

**Pros:** full history preserved, all individual commits bisectable on main. The two-parent merge commit gives git the information it needs to detect "this branch is already merged" for future merges.
**Cons:** noisier history (one merge commit per PR + every individual commit).

## 3. Rebase and merge

GitHub replays A, B, C onto main's tip as if they had always been there. No merge commit.

```
main:    M1 ──── M2 ──── A' ──── B' ──── C'
```

- A', B', C' are NEW commits (different SHA than original A, B, C — git rewrites parent pointers)
- All single-parent
- Linear history; looks like the work happened directly on main

**Pros:** clean linear history without the "extra" merge commits.
**Cons:** rewrites SHAs (problematic if anyone had pulled the feature branch), no record that the work came from a PR.

## What just bit us

I pushed #334 as a **merge commit** locally — its parents were dev-tip + main-tip. That was deliberate: I wanted main's tip to become an ancestor of dev so future dev → main merges would see "main is already absorbed" and just fast-forward.

GitHub merged #334 with **Squash**. That collapsed my carefully-crafted merge commit into a regular single-parent commit. The new commit on dev has the right *file content* (took dev's seed) but no parent link to main. From git's perspective, main's commits are still "outside" dev — so #333 still sees a conflict.

## When to pick which

- **Squash**: trivial 1-PR-1-commit work, throwaway code, anything where history doesn't matter. The default in most repos because clean history > granular history for most projects.
- **Merge commit**: when you specifically want to record "branch X was merged into branch Y" with both histories preserved. **The only correct choice for "promote dev to main" or similar branch-to-branch merges** where you need git to know that one branch is now a subset of another.
- **Rebase**: when you want linear history AND you're sure no one else has pulled the feature branch.

The rule of thumb that would have saved us a step: **branch-to-branch promotion = merge commit; PR-to-branch = squash usually fine.**

> AGENT

Great question. The trick is git **doesn't compare file contents** when deciding what to merge — it walks the **commit graph** (the parent-pointer tree). And the squash created two histories that look totally different to git, even though the files are identical.

## What just happened, drawn out

Before the squash, dev was 138 commits ahead of main:

```
main:  M1 ── M2 ──── (LAST COMMON ANCESTOR)
                       \
dev:                    A ── B ── C ── ... 138 commits ... ── DEV_TIP
```

When you squashed dev → main, GitHub:
1. Computed the *diff* between M2 and DEV_TIP (just the file changes)
2. Created **one new commit `S`** on main containing that diff
3. `S`'s only parent is M2 — **not** DEV_TIP

So now:

```
main:  M1 ── M2 ──── S      ← main has 1 new commit (S)
                \
                 A ── B ── C ── ... ── DEV_TIP    ← dev still has its 138 commits
```

**`S` and DEV_TIP have the same file contents but they are completely different commits** (different SHAs, different parents). From git's bird's-eye view of the graph:

- The last commit they share is **M2** (way back at the start)
- After M2, main has its own commit (S)
- After M2, dev has its own 138 commits

When you next try to merge dev → main, git asks: "what's new on each side since M2?"
- On main: S (touched a bunch of files)
- On dev: 138 commits (touched the same files)

Same files modified independently on both sides → **conflict**, even though the end state is identical.

## Why the "sync back" fixes it

When you merge main → dev with a real merge commit, you create:

```
main:  M1 ── M2 ── S
                    \
dev:    A ── B ── ... DEV_TIP ── SYNC    ← SYNC has TWO parents: DEV_TIP and S
```

Now `S` is in dev's ancestry. Next time you compute "last common ancestor of dev and main":
- They share **S** now (via the SYNC commit's parent pointer)
- After S: main has nothing new, dev has SYNC
- No conflict possible — SYNC is a fast-forward target

## The cleanest analogy

Imagine you and a friend both transcribe the same book independently. When you compare your work, every word matches. But neither of you has read the other's transcription. If a publisher asks "merge your two manuscripts into one", they can't just trust that you're identical — they have to go line by line. If you both wrote "page 5" by hand, the publisher sees two competing page-5s and asks you to pick one. The fact that they're identical is irrelevant; the publisher's process compares paths, not destinations.

Git is that publisher. The "sync back" is you reading your friend's manuscript so you can sign off and say "yep mine matches" — recording that signoff in a way the publisher trusts.

## TL;DR

- Squash gave you the **right content** on main but **broke the family tree**.
- Git's merge logic walks the family tree, not the file contents.
- One throwaway sync merge stitches the family tree back together so future merges fast-forward instead of recomputing what got applied where.

> AGENT

## The pattern, every release

```
1. Develop on dev (PRs into dev with squash — that's fine)
2. When ready to release:
     PR dev → main  →  SQUASH merge   (main gets "Release vX.Y.Z" commit)
     (optionally) tag main with vX.Y.Z
3. Immediately after:
     PR main → dev  →  CREATE A MERGE COMMIT   (not squash)
     The PR contains zero file changes — just one merge commit
     Title it something like "Sync main vX.Y.Z back into dev"
4. Back to step 1 for the next release
```

That's it. Two PRs per release, executed back-to-back. Step 3 takes 30 seconds.

## Why each step is shaped the way it is

| Step | Strategy | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | **Squash** | Collapses 100+ commits into one. Main reads as a clean release timeline — `git log main` shows "v1.0", "v1.1", "v1.2"… one line per release. |
| 3 | **Merge commit** | Adds a single merge commit to dev whose second parent IS the squash commit on main. Stitches the family tree so future dev → main fast-forwards. |

If you skip step 3, every subsequent step 2 hits the same conflict re-resolution dance we just did.

## What the sync PR actually looks like

When you open step 3:

- **Files changed:** 0
- **Commits:** 1 merge commit
- **Diff size:** empty

GitHub usually displays it as "This branch has no conflicts with the base branch" and the merge button shows "Create a merge commit" available. You click it. Done.

The reason the diff is empty: main and dev already have identical *file contents* at that moment. The merge commit is purely a graph-shape change — it adds a parent pointer, nothing else.

## Bonus convention if you want to lean in

Treat the squash message format on step 2 as your release notes:

```
Release v1.5: Analyst workspace cutover + run-cap improvements

- Cut over `/` → `/analyst/` (#331)
- Demo question delete admin guard (#321)
- Partial runs count against cap (#325)
- Target preservation across runs (#324)
- ...
```

Then tag it: `git tag -a v1.5 cfc5732 -m "Release v1.5" && git push origin v1.5`. GitHub will surface it as a Release in the sidebar. The squash message becomes your release notes automatically.

```

Want me to open it? It's the cleanup that unbricks future releases.

> AGENT

Honest opinion: **for your team's size and release cadence, the dev/main split is overhead you don't need.** Industry default for a small team shipping a SaaS demo is trunk-based — everyone PRs to `main`, no separate dev branch. Two-branch models exist for libraries with explicit release versions or products with rare, coordinated releases. You're closer to the former in intent (you want main = versions) but neither in actual practice (you deploy whenever).

Here are the three live options, ranked by what I'd actually recommend:

## Option A — Trunk-based (most modern teams)

One branch: `main`.

```
PRs → main (squash, usually)
push to main → CI runs → auto-deploy to staging
git tag v1.5 + push tag → CI runs → auto-deploy to prod
```

Eliminates the entire "promote dev to main" dance and all its conflict bookkeeping. Releases become tags, not merges. Each tag's commit message is the release notes; GitHub Releases UI surfaces them.

**Why this is the modern default:** less branch state to reason about, no sync-back PRs, simpler mental model. Used by most modern web/SaaS teams (GitHub, Vercel, Linear, basically all the YC product companies). Continuous deployment shops insist on it.

**What it costs you:** you'd need to swap CI to deploy-on-tag instead of deploy-on-merge-to-main. ~30 lines of YAML change in `.github/workflows/`.

## Option B — Keep dev/main, switch to rebase-and-merge for promotions

If you want to keep the dev branch but never deal with sync-back again:

```
PRs → dev (squash, fine)
when releasing: PR dev → main, REBASE-AND-MERGE   ← not squash
optionally tag main
```

Rebase-and-merge takes dev's commits and replays them onto main one by one. Same SHAs end up on main as on dev (well, same content with new SHAs — but git treats them as a fast-forwardable line). Next dev → main: nothing's changed, no conflict.

**Cost:** main accumulates every dev commit (your "versions are single commits" wish goes away).
**Win:** zero sync-back overhead forever.

## Option C — Current model, but with the sync-back as a hard convention

What I described in the previous message. Squash dev → main for clean release commits, immediately follow with merge-commit main → dev sync.

**Cost:** every release is two PRs (release + sync). Easy to forget the sync. When you forget, next release conflicts.
**Win:** main reads exactly like you want (one commit per version).

## My recommendation

**Option A** — go trunk-based. Reasons:

1. You're a 2-3 person team shipping rapidly. The ceremony of dev/main mostly costs you, doesn't protect you.
2. You already have a staging hostname (`dev.elijahintelligence.com`) separate from prod (`demo.elijahintelligence.com`) — you don't NEED the branch separation to do staging/prod isolation; the hostnames + tag-gated prod deploys do it.
3. Your "main = versions" intent is better served by **tags** than by merge commits. Tags are immutable named pointers, surface as Releases in GitHub UI, are what tools like Sentry / Datadog / package managers expect.
4. The "do dev → main + sync back" dance is exactly the kind of thing teams stop doing as they grow, because it's overhead nobody enforces consistently.

**If you don't want to refactor CI right now**: do Option C consistently, document the sync-back step in a runbook (or automate it with a GitHub Action that opens the sync PR automatically after every main push). It works fine, you just have to remember it.

**Don't do Option B** — it's the "least bad middle ground" but you give up your stated goal (clean release commits on main) without getting the simplicity of Option A.

Want me to draft the trunk-based migration as a PR? It'd be a small change to `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml` (swap `deploy-prod`'s trigger from `ref_name == 'main'` to `startsWith(ref, 'refs/tags/v')`) and a one-time `git branch -d dev` after everyone's PRs catch up.

> AGENT

Found it. Here's what happened:

**When you merged PR #333**, GitHub's "delete branch after merge" option deleted the `dev` branch. (Visible in my push log earlier — `[new branch]   sumeet/promote-merge-from-main -> dev` means dev didn't exist when I pushed; I recreated it.)

**GitHub's behavior when a base branch is deleted**: every open PR that targeted that branch gets auto-retargeted to the repo's default branch (which is `main` per CLAUDE.md). That's what swept the 4 dev-bound PRs (#245, #318, #323, #332) over to main.

**GitHub doesn't auto-undo** when the deleted branch is recreated. So they're stuck on main until manually retargeted.

Fix is one command per PR. Doing all four:

> TOOL

tool_use Bash
id: toolu_01Wns2CW96xDQkjSBJaQiopV
```json
{
  "command": "for n in 245 318 323 332; do\n  echo \"=== retargeting #$n to dev ===\"\n  gh pr edit $n --base dev 2>&1 | tail -2\ndone && echo --- && gh pr list --state open --json number,baseRefName,title --jq '.[] | \"\\(.number)  → \\(.baseRefName)  \\(.title[:60])\"' 2>&1 | head",
  "description": "Retarget the 4 PRs back to dev + verify"
}
```

> AGENT

All four retargeted to dev. The PR list is back to its normal shape — only #338 targets a feature branch (probably a stacked PR; that's intentional), everything else targets dev.

**To prevent this recurring:** in your repo settings, you can either:
- Disable "automatically delete head branches" for `dev` specifically (it's the integration branch, not a head branch)
- Or just remember to uncheck the "Delete branch" checkbox when merging the next dev → main release PR

The first is the more durable fix. Settings → General → "Automatically delete head branches" — toggle off, OR add a branch protection rule on `dev` that prevents deletion.

    permissions:

        run: |
          curl -sfH "Authorization: token ${GH_TOKEN}" \
            -H "Accept: application/vnd.github.v3.raw" \
            "https://api.github.com/repos/${{ github.repository }}/contents/compose.prod.yml?ref=${{ github.sha }}" \
            -o /home/elijah/prod/compose.prod.yml

      - name: Pull and restart prod
        working-directory: /home/elijah/prod
        run: |
          export ELIJAH_IMAGE=${{ env.REGISTRY }}/${{ env.IMAGE_NAME }}:main
          docker compose -f compose.prod.yml pull
          docker compose -f compose.prod.yml run --rm api uv run python -m tools.cli.main storage-init
